episode_title: The Most Overlooked Part of Customer Experience | Joe Macleod

real_qa.q: Why do most businesses fail to intentionally design customer endings despite focusing heavily on beginnings and middles?
real_qa.r: Historically, the Industrial Revolution distanced consumers from product creators, and digitization has been applied to onboarding and usage but not offboarding—most brands still require customers to call a phone line for cancellation. Additionally, business culture has always framed endings as negative events rather than opportunities for meaning and trust-building.
real_qa.requete: why businesses ignore customer endings design

real_qa.q: What are the eight types of endings that products can have according to Endineering framework?
real_qa.r: The eight types include credit out endings, time out endings, task or event completion endings, and cultural endings—such as fashion representing a cultural ending. Each type frames the customer relationship differently and requires distinct design approaches based on the business model.

real_qa.q: How do different transaction models like payment before versus payment after affect the power dynamic and ending experience?
real_qa.r: Payment before (flights, trains) leaves customers with no leverage at the end; payment after (restaurants) gives customers maximum leverage. Restaurants excel at pushing toward good endings because they want to ensure customer satisfaction before payment, whereas subscription models with continuous payment often lack reflection moments that could strengthen brand relationships.
real_qa.requete: payment before after transaction ending leverage

real_qa.q: What are the seven phases of offboarding that make up the narrative structure of a product ending?
real_qa.r: The seven phases range from the crack of doubt—when the customer first considers leaving—through to rebirth, which occurs in the aftermath and determines whether the customer is ready to engage again or purchase another product. Each phase requires intentional design to add meaning and emotional resolution.

real_qa.q: Did a major telecoms company's simple app-based offboarding increase customer churn after launch?
real_qa.r: No—when a large telecoms company built a smooth, simple ending feature in their app to replace hard retention calls, senior management feared mass exodus, but the number of departing customers remained the same. The key difference was that customers left with much better sentiment about the brand, demonstrating that making endings simpler does not increase churn.
